tasks.question: What has to happen to a node before a kernel upgrade?

attempts.text: Before a kernel upgrade, nodes must be drained without exception. This means the node is cordoned first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it, then the running pods are evicted and wait for them to reschedule elsewhere. This ensures the node is not serving traffic during the upgrade, as an in-place kernel upgrade on a node still serving traffic has caused two of the three longest outages. After the packages are installed, the node must be rebooted to boot the new kernel version properly [1][2].

citations.title: Node maintenance
citations.quote:
## Kernel upgrades

Nodes are drained before any kernel upgrade, without exception. An in-place kernel
upgrade on a node that is still serving traffic has caused two of our three
longest outages.

Reboot the node after the packages are installed. A kernel that is installed but
not booted reports the new version to the package manager and the old version to
the running system, which makes every subsequent audit wrong.

citations.title: Node maintenance
citations.quote:
## Draining a node

Cordon the node first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it. Cordoning is
not eviction: pods already running keep running, and the node keeps serving
traffic until they are moved.

Once the node is cordoned, evict the running pods and wait for them to reschedule
elsewhere. Eviction respects pod disruption budgets, so a workload that declares
one will be moved a replica at a time.

tasks.question: What happens to a webhook that cannot be delivered for a whole day?

attempts.text: A webhook delivery that cannot be delivered for a whole day is retried using exponential backoff with jitter, capped at twenty-four hours. After this period, the delivery is moved to a dead letter queue and the customer is notified by email [1].

citations.title: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
heading_path: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
citations.quote:
## Decision

Webhook deliveries are enqueued and delivered by a separate worker pool.

The queue is durable, so a delivery survives a deploy. Retries use exponential
backoff with jitter, capped at twenty-four hours, after which the delivery is
moved to a dead letter queue and the customer is notified by email.

tasks.question: What caused the checkout latency incident INC-2451?

attempts.text: The checkout latency incident INC-2451 was caused by connection pool exhaustion in the payments service. This exhaustion was triggered by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run. The merchant onboarding campaign had increased the merchant count past the pool size for the first time, causing the job's connection usage to cross a threshold that had not been documented. This led to the checkout p99 latency rising from 240 ms to 9 seconds for 47 minutes, although no requests were lost [2][3].

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## Summary

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.

## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.

tasks.question: What is the per-service connection ceiling that RB-114 step three tells me to compare against?

attempts.text: The per-service connection ceiling that RB-114 step three tells you to compare against is 400 connections. This ceiling is enforced at the database by a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused rather than queued [2][7].

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

2. Check whether the replica count changed in the last six hours. Each replica
   opens its own pool, so the connections a service asks for are the pool size
   multiplied by the replica count.

3. **Compare that product against the per-service connection ceiling.** The
   ceiling is a database setting and is listed in the service limits reference.
   If the product exceeds it, reduce the replica count until it does not. This is
   the step that resolves the common case, and it resolves it without a restart.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

tasks.question: In INC-3187 the reconciliation job was running. Was it what saturated the pool?

attempts.text: No, the reconciliation job was not what saturated the pool in INC-3187. The postmortem states that the nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled and ran against a dedicated pool that was correctly sized, so the saturation was not caused by the job. Instead, the saturation was caused by a deployment that increased the payments service replica count from four to nine, which led to the total requested connections exceeding the per-service connection ceiling at the database, causing the ninth replica's connections to be refused [1].

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What happened

The nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled after the capacity review signed it
off. It ran against the dedicated pool that INC-2451's actions created, and that
pool was correctly sized. The saturation was not the job.

A deployment three hours earlier had raised the payments service replica count
from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service
connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service — so nine
replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling and the
ninth replica's connections were refused.

tasks.question: How many replicas can a payments service run on the default pool size before it hits the connection ceiling?

attempts.text: The payments service can run up to nine replicas on the default pool size before it hits the connection ceiling. The default pool size per replica is 40 connections, and the per-service connection ceiling is 400. Since 40 connections per replica multiplied by 10 replicas equals 400, the ceiling is reached at ten replicas. Therefore, the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any service using the default pool size [5].

tasks.question: A service is returning connection errors and I am about to restart it. Should I?

attempts.text: No, you should not restart the service first. According to RB-114, if the service is returning connection errors due to a saturated connection pool, you should first check the pool utilization per replica, the replica count changes, and compare the product of pool size and replica count against the per-service connection ceiling. Restarting the service clears the symptom but destroys the evidence, and the incident will recur on the next run of whatever was holding the connections open [2]. The runbook explicitly advises not to restart the service first in this situation [2].

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

2. Check whether the replica count changed in the last six hours. Each replica
   opens its own pool, so the connections a service asks for are the pool size
   multiplied by the replica count.

3. **Compare that product against the per-service connection ceiling.** The
   ceiling is a database setting and is listed in the service limits reference.
   If the product exceeds it, reduce the replica count until it does not. This is
   the step that resolves the common case, and it resolves it without a restart.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

tasks.question: Can I stop the connection errors by raising the pool size?

attempts.text: No, you should not raise the pool size to make the connection errors stop. The pool size ceiling is per service and enforced at the database level. tasks.question: Both INC-2451 and INC-3187 exhausted a connection pool. What was different about the cause?

attempts.text:
The cause of the connection pool exhaustion differed between INC-2451 and INC-3187 as follows:

- INC-2451 was caused by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run. The merchant count had increased past the pool size for the first time, causing the job's connection usage to cross a threshold that was not documented. Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause, and the job was not scheduled to retry, so the incident would have recurred within the hour [5][7].

- INC-3187 was caused by a deployment that increased the payments service replica count from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service. Therefore, nine replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling, and the ninth replica's connections were refused. The nightly reconciliation job was not the cause in this incident [3].

In summary, INC-2451 was due to the reconciliation job's connection usage exceeding the pool size because of increased merchant count, while INC-3187 was due to the replica count increase causing the total requested connections to exceed the database connection ceiling [3][5][7].

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.

citations.quote:

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.
